hook: SCP-1427 opens with one of the most uncomfortable containment arrangements you'll find: the Foundation works with North Korea's army and deliberately keeps the state exactly as it is. The object itself is a bronze slab that wipes out human consciousness, but the article is really about what containment costs and who is made to pay. Expect an ethics dissent and an archaeological report rather than action.
whyItMatters: This is a strong example of a file whose horror lives in the procedures rather than the object: because a totalitarian population has to surround the artifact, geopolitics itself becomes a containment measure. The Ethics Committee dissent gives the Foundation's greater-good logic an articulate critic from inside, turning that logic against the decision. The closing site report then widens the frame far beyond the twentieth century.
thingsToNotice:
The immunity rule is the hinge: people high in authoritarian submission resist the signal, so the staffing criteria read like a personality test and the procedures forbid anyone from talking the guards out of their beliefs. The stele's history runs from Algeria through Italy, Germany and the USSR to Pyongyang, and the 1957 activation at Kyshtym was stopped from ending humanity only by the nature of the Soviet system itself.

Two dissenting site supervisors argue the Foundation could condition a population of the required size on its own instead of holding more than twenty million people in place, and call the refusal an abdication. The Tamanrasset report then reveals the object's makers: a giant, six-fingered hominid provisionally named Homo sapiens descensus, which seems to have used it to subjugate early humans, at a site scarred by a failed nuclear blast about 70,000 years ago and later stripped of descensus remains by humans. Because these artifacts appear to block fission, the team recommends conventional means and the recovery of the lost inscribed casing.
